theme: Steadfast love reaches to the heavens, common grace celebrated
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 36:5-12 slowly, twice. This is the second half of Psalm 36, the first half describes the wicked, the second half praises God’s steadfast love. Today’s portion is the praise section. Read it as the appropriate response to all we have seen in Genesis 4-11: in a world of human wickedness, God’s love reaches to the heavens.
settingTheScene:
We have just spent six days walking through the bleakest portion of the early Bible, Cain’s murder of Abel, the universal spread of death in Genesis 5, the corruption of all flesh in Genesis 6, the flood, the post-flood failure of Noah, and finally the pride of Babel. The human story so far has not been encouraging. We have seen humanity in rebellion at every scale: individual, family, civilization, world.

Today’s psalm reminds us that the bleakness of human sin is not the last word. God’s steadfast love is bigger. His faithfulness reaches to the clouds. His righteousness is like the mountains. His justice is like the great deep. In a world of Cains and Lamechs and Babels, God’s love runs deeper than human evil ever can.
observation: Verse 5: “Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.” The vertical scale of God’s love matches the vertical attempts at Babel, but God truly reaches the heavens.
Verse 6: God’s righteousness is “like the mountains of God,” his judgments “like the great deep.” The natural world is the measure of his moral attributes.
Verse 6 ends with a beautiful inclusion: “man and beast you save, O LORD.” Common grace is in view, God’s care extends to all creatures.
Verse 7: “How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings.” Image of a mother bird sheltering her young.
Verses 8-9 use feast and water imagery: “they feast on the abundance of your house… For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.”
Verse 9 contains one of the most theologically rich lines in the Psalms: “in your light do we see light.” Knowledge of God comes through God himself.
The psalm closes with a prayer that God will preserve his people from the wicked and ensure the downfall of evildoers, fitting after the chapters we just read.
interpretation:
Psalm 36:5-12 is one of the most expansive descriptions of God’s love in the entire Psalter. After the first half of the psalm describes the wicked, those who flatter themselves, who plot evil on their beds, who do not reject what is evil, the second half lifts our eyes upward to behold something greater than human wickedness: the steadfast love of God himself.

Notice the vertical movement of verse 5: “Your steadfast love, O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness to the clouds.” Right after we have just read about humanity building a tower whose “top is in the heavens” (Genesis 11:4), this psalm announces that God’s love is what actually reaches the heavens. The Babel-builders tried to make their name reach to the clouds. They failed. But God’s faithfulness already reaches there. The human pride that tried to bridge heaven and earth from below is unnecessary, because God’s love has already bridged it from above.

The next image is equally striking. “Your righteousness is like the mountains of God, your judgments are like the great deep.” God’s character is given the scale of creation itself. His righteousness is mountainous, solid, immovable, towering. His judgments are deep, beyond human plumbing, profound, unsearchable. We do not measure God’s morality by our own intuitions. We measure our intuitions by his unchanging character. And both of these, the heights of his love and the depths of his judgments, are realities we can stake our lives on.

Then verse 6 ends with a sentence that lands with extra weight after the readings of Unit 2: “Man and beast you save, O LORD.” Save. The Hebrew word is yasha, the same root from which we get the name Yeshua, Jesus. God saves not only humans but animals. He cares for all his creatures. After the flood narrative, where animals were taken into the ark, after the Noahic Covenant which explicitly includes “every living creature”, this verse rings with theological weight. God’s saving care extends across all his creation.

Verse 7 introduces one of the most tender images in the Psalter. “How precious is your steadfast love, O God! The children of mankind take refuge in the shadow of your wings.” This is the image of a mother bird sheltering her chicks under her outstretched wings. Jesus will use this very image later in his lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37): “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you would not!” The God of Psalm 36 is the God of Christ, the one who longs to gather his people under his protection.

Then comes a feast. Verse 8: “They feast on the abundance of your house, and you give them drink from the river of your delights.” This is hospitality. God does not merely tolerate his people; he feeds them lavishly. The “river of your delights” (Hebrew Eden, the very word!) recalls the garden of Eden and its rivers of life. What was lost in the Fall is offered again to those who take refuge in God. The original garden has not been forgotten; it is being recovered for those who come to him.

Then verse 9 lands as one of the most theologically dense lines in all of Scripture: “For with you is the fountain of life; in your light do we see light.” Both parts of this verse contain entire theologies. Life itself flows from God, he is the fountain, the source, the spring. Apart from him, there is no life. And we see light only by his light. Knowledge of God is not human achievement; it is divine self-revelation. We do not climb up to see God; he shines down so that we can see him. This is the doctrine of revelation in eight words.

The psalm closes with a prayer that God will continue his steadfast love to those who know him, and that the wicked will not have the final word. This is exactly the right prayer after Unit 2. We have seen the wicked, Cain, the world before the flood, the Babel-builders. We have seen God’s patience and grace. And now we pray, with the psalmist, that God’s steadfast love will continue, and that the trajectory of the wicked will end in judgment, while the trajectory of those who know God will end in light.
connection: Six days ago we read about Cain, whose anger was not ruled. Today’s psalm describes those who “have no fear of God before their eyes” (the first half of Psalm 36, not in our reading), Cain’s spiritual descendants. But after the description of wickedness comes the description of God’s love, and it is overwhelming. After all we have read in Unit 2, the spread of sin, the flood, Babel, this psalm is the appropriate worship. Yes, the world is full of human wickedness. But God’s love reaches to the heavens. His faithfulness to the clouds. His righteousness like mountains. His judgments like the great deep. The God of common grace, who preserves creation under the Noahic Covenant, is the God whose love is bigger than every evil we have witnessed.
application:
The psalmist’s response to wickedness is not despair, and not vengeance. It is to lift his eyes to the steadfast love of God. This is a learnable habit. When you read the news, when you face conflict in relationships, when you see injustice that grieves you, you have a choice. You can let your soul shrink down to the size of the wickedness in front of you, or you can lift your eyes to the love of God that reaches to the heavens. The wicked are real. So is God’s steadfast love. Choose which one you will let define your day.

Practically, take verse 9 with you today. “In your light do we see light.” We do not see clearly by our own effort. We see by God’s light. This applies to almost every dimension of the Christian life. We do not understand Scripture by our own intelligence; we understand it by the illumination of the Spirit. We do not pray well by our own ability; we pray well by the Spirit who teaches us to cry “Abba, Father.” We do not love well by our own willpower; we love well by the love of God poured into our hearts. The light is his, given to us. Receive it.

And consider the image of taking refuge in the shadow of God’s wings. In a world where everything feels exposed, where reputations can be destroyed by a single tweet, where lives can be unraveled by a single accident, God offers shadow. Hiddenness. Protection. The Christian is not asked to be impressive in the world’s eyes. The Christian is invited to be hidden under God’s wings, fed at his table, given to drink from his river. This is your inheritance in Christ. Today, claim it.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for steadfast love that is bigger than the wickedness you see, including your own.
Ask him to hide you in the shadow of his wings today.
Pray that in his light you would see yourself, the world, and Christ more truly.
